summary: The stated fix (confirm_merge() returning a distinct 'ambiguous' flag so a transient gh failure skips-with-warning instead of triggering a false revert) is correct, well-motivated, and covered by a real regression test that passes, along with the missing-target_repo and blame/parent-lookup-failure incident-recording improvements. However, live-reproducing the exact scenario this feature exists to handle (a phase-plan file accumulating more than one bypassed/false self-report) surfaces a genuine, unverified-by-the-test-suite bug in audit_and_correct_plan_file()/blame_line(): reverting an earlier violation in a plan file can delete lines from the on-disk working copy (when the parent revision lacks completed_by_task/evidence), which shifts the line numbers of every later block in the same file. The next loop iteration computes status_idx against the now-shrunk on-disk file but calls `git blame HEAD` (HEAD is unchanged, still the original larger file) with that shifted line number, blaming the wrong line entirely. In a reproduction with two bypassed phases in one file, this produced a corrupted commit hash (a literal '^' boundary-commit marker mistakenly concatenated into the hash string), caused the second violation's revert to abort with a spurious 'parent revision could not be read' incident, left the second phase's false self-report in place un-reverted, and still auto-committed+pushed to master with the corrupted hash baked into the permanent commit message/incident record. This directly undermines the feature's own audit-trail integrity goal and would let a real bypassed phase survive an audit run while reporting a misleading incident. Given this is tier1 (autonomous merge on approval) and the bug manifests in exactly the multi-violation-per-file case this feature is built to catch, this should not be merged as-is.
issues: Confirmed logic bug (reproduced live, not from the diff alone): when a single plan file has more than one phase falsely self-reporting done, audit_and_correct_plan_file()'s while-loop reverts the first violation (which can delete lines from the on-disk file when the parent lacks completed_by_task/evidence), then re-reads the mutated file and computes the next violation's status_idx against it -- but blame_line() blames that line number against `git blame HEAD`, where HEAD still reflects the pre-revert (larger) file. The line-number mismatch causes git blame to attribute the wrong commit, in the reproduction yielding a corrupted hash string containing a stray boundary-commit '^' character, which then fails the parent-lookup step and leaves the second violation un-reverted while still committing+pushing the (correct) first revert plus a misleading 'could not auto-revert' incident to master.

No regression test exercises more than one violation in the same plan file, so this bug shipped despite the otherwise-thorough test suite (10 scenarios, all passing) -- the multi-violation-per-file case is exactly the scenario --audit-plans exists to handle over the lifetime of a real, recurring cron-run script.

Minor, lower severity: audit_and_correct_plan_file()'s 'found but NOT auto-corrected' incidents (blame/parent-lookup/fabricated-block failures) are only ever surfaced via stderr log() and the process's own stdout JSON -- if that plan file's only violation is one of these un-auto-corrected cases, changed_any stays False, so commit_and_push_audit() is never called and the incident is never persisted into git history (only into whatever captures this invocation's stdout, e.g. a cron log). This is a smaller version of the same 'convention, not enforcement' gap the module docstring says this feature is meant to close.
